meta.title: Agent Memory
meta.thesis: Agent Memory is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A support-refund agent must remember customer preferences without storing sensitive payment details. By the end, they should be able to build or review memory policy plus retrieval test for a billing-support agent, measure repeat-question rate, and catch the failure where private card fragments get saved as long-term memory.

mentalMap.title: Agent Memory: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Separate memory types, provenance, retrieval, and correction before letting an agent remember anything durable.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Agent memory is product state with governance; it is not a transcript dump, a context window, or a replacement for source-of-truth data.

modules.title: Memory is durable product state
modules.sub: Remembering changes future behavior after the prompt is gone.
modules.summary: An agent memory should be deliberate, scoped, and reviewable.
objectives: Define agent memory separately from context window and RAG.
Explain why bad memories become durable bugs.
Identify the user-visible behavior memory should improve.

blocks.title: Memory outlives the current turn

spans.text: Problem anchor: a tutor remembers that a learner “hates math” after one frustrated joke. Two weeks later it avoids useful equations in every lesson. The bug is not a bad answer; it is durable state that should never have been stored as fact.

Memory is information persisted so later runs behave differently. Thread history, workflow checkpoints, RAG documents, and application database records can all inform an agent, but long-term memory needs a narrower contract.
Before storing anything, finish the sentence “This memory will improve future behavior by...”

blocks.analogy: Memory is a sticky note on the product, not a thought passing through the model.

blocks.title: Worked memory boundary: learner preference or temporary mood

spans.text: The learner says, “Use Python examples when possible; I am preparing for backend interviews.” That can become a procedural preference with source turn ID and confidence.
The learner also says, “I am done, this is impossible.” That should not become a durable ability label. It may influence the current support response, but it should expire with the thread.

items.text: Classify the statement as preference, fact, event, or transient mood.
Decide whether later sessions should use it.
Store source turn, timestamp, confidence, and namespace.
Expose it for correction or deletion.

blocks.title: Memory boundary
blocks.prompt: Which item is safest to store as long-term memory?

options.text: The user makes one sarcastic comment about being bad at math.
The user explicitly says they prefer Python examples for future lessons.
A retrieved policy document says refunds take 30 days.

blocks.explanation: Long-term memory is for durable user or task continuity, not transient mood or external facts better handled by RAG.

modules.title: Classify short-term, semantic, episodic, and procedural memory
modules.sub: Different memory types need different storage and retrieval rules.
objectives: Distinguish thread state from long-term memory.
Classify semantic, episodic, and procedural memories.
Choose RAG or database records when memory is the wrong tool.

blocks.title: Not every remembered thing belongs in the same place

spans.text: Short-term thread state keeps a multi-step run coherent: messages, tool results, plan, and checkpoints. Semantic memory stores durable facts such as “the team uses Postgres.” Episodic memory records events. Procedural memory stores preferences or instructions.
Use the application database for canonical records like subscription plan or lesson completion. Use RAG for source documents. Use workflow state for exact progress through side effects.
Ask “who owns the truth?” If the answer is billing, docs, or workflow engine, do not store it as free-form agent memory.

blocks.analogy: A memory system is a filing cabinet with labeled drawers, not one bottomless box.

options.name: Thread state

cells.text: Current run messages, plan, tool results.
Can become bloated context if never summarized.

options.whenToUse: Use during a single conversation or graph run.

options.name: Semantic memory
options.whenToUse: Use when a fact should affect later sessions.

options.name: Procedural memory

cells.text: Can conflict with current task or policy.

options.whenToUse: Use when user wants repeated behavior.

blocks.title: Memory classification
blocks.prompt: Where should an account’s paid plan usually live?

options.text: As an inferred long-term memory from chat text.
In the application database, then be read as needed.
Only inside the model context window forever.

blocks.explanation: Canonical business records should not be free-form memories.

modules.title: Extract memories with provenance and policy
modules.sub: A memory extractor proposes; product policy decides.
modules.summary: The write path is where memory governance begins.
objectives: Create candidate memories from turns or tool results.

blocks.title: The extractor is not the authority

spans.text: A model can propose candidate memories, but product code should decide whether to store them. The policy layer checks sensitivity, explicitness, namespace, confidence, retention, and whether the memory duplicates a canonical record.
Provenance matters because a user may later ask “why do you think that?” The system should point to the source turn or tool result and allow correction.
Store “who said it, when, in what context, and why we accepted it” beside the memory value.

blocks.analogy: Memory extraction is intake; policy is the editor.

blocks.title: Case study: extracting only durable preferences

spans.text: After a lesson chat, the extractor proposes three candidates: prefers Python examples, currently tired, and company uses Postgres. The policy accepts Python preference because it is explicit and future-useful, rejects tired as transient, and routes company stack to project memory only if the workspace owner allows it.
Each accepted memory stores source turn ID and a status of active, so it can be corrected later.

items.text: Generate candidate memory with type and confidence.
Reject sensitive, transient, or unsupported items.
Write accepted memory under a user or project namespace.

blocks.title: Write policy
blocks.prompt: Why should memory records include source metadata?

options.text: So the model can ignore the current user request.
So users and operators can inspect, correct, or delete the memory later.
So all memories become public search results.

blocks.explanation: Provenance is the path to trust and correction.

modules.title: Retrieve narrowly into the current task
modules.sub: Memory recall should be scoped, ranked, and explainable.
modules.summary: Memory retrieval is a precision problem.
objectives: Use namespace isolation for memory search.
Filter active memories by task relevance.
Predict how bad retrieval changes an answer.

blocks.title: Memory should enter context on purpose

spans.text: At query time, the agent should search only the appropriate namespace, filter active memories, and retrieve items relevant to the current task. A preference about Python examples should not appear in a billing dispute unless it matters.
Memory text should be labeled as user preference, inferred fact, or prior event. The prompt should not let memory outrank current user instructions or policy.
If you cannot explain why a memory was inserted into the prompt, remove it from that run.

blocks.title: Tiny typed memory store with scoped retrieval
blocks.explanation: The retrieval code isolates users, ignores expired items, and only injects preferences when the task can use them.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before running it, predict which preference appears for user u1.
predictThenReveal.answer: It prints Python for u1 and TypeScript for u2. The expired transient memory never appears, and namespaces prevent cross-user leakage.

blocks.title: Recall scope
blocks.prompt: What is the most serious bug in memory retrieval?

options.text: Using a list instead of a database in a toy example.
Retrieving another user’s memory into the current prompt.
Storing timestamps with memories.

blocks.explanation: Namespace isolation is a safety boundary, not a convenience.

modules.title: Let users inspect, correct, and forget
modules.sub: Memory needs lifecycle controls, not only embeddings.
modules.summary: Memory is production-ready when it can be governed over time.
objectives: Test memory write and recall failures.

blocks.title: Memory governance is part of the feature

spans.text: A memory UI or API should let users see important memories, correct false ones, delete sensitive ones, and understand whether a memory was inferred or explicitly stated.

Regression tests should include over-memory, under-memory, namespace leakage, stale preference, and correction scenarios. Production traces should show which memories were retrieved and how they influenced the answer.
A memory feature is incomplete if the only way to fix a false memory is to beg the model to forget.

blocks.title: Verify AI output that uses memory

spans.text: Review answers that include recalled memories with these checks.

items.text: The answer labels memory as preference or prior context rather than external fact.
The recalled memory belongs to the correct user or workspace namespace.
Current user instructions and safety policy override older memory.
The memory has provenance and can be corrected or deleted.
The answer still cites RAG or database sources for factual claims.

blocks.title: Memory lifecycle
blocks.prompt: A user says “stop remembering that I prefer short answers.” What should the product do?

options.text: Only add a new prompt saying to ignore the old memory.
Update or delete the stored preference in the memory store.
Tell the user memory cannot be changed.

blocks.explanation: Correction belongs in the memory system, not just in a one-turn prompt.

agent.label: Agent
agent.laymanDefinition: A software loop that plans, observes results, and may use tools to pursue a goal.
agent.technicalNote: Agent designs need explicit loop boundaries, stop conditions, permissions, state contracts, and evaluation surfaces before autonomy is useful.

tool.label: Tool
tool.laymanDefinition: An external capability the model can request, such as search, code execution, retrieval, or a business API.
tool.technicalNote: Tools require schemas, authorization, error handling, audit logs, and tests because natural-language intent is not execution permission.

state.label: State
state.laymanDefinition: The working information carried between steps of an agent workflow.
state.technicalNote: State should separate durable facts, transient scratch work, approvals, tool results, and failure metadata so retries and handoffs remain understandable.

memory.label: Memory
memory.laymanDefinition: Information saved across turns or sessions for future use.
memory.technicalNote: Agent memory needs scope, freshness, deletion, privacy controls, and evaluation so saved context helps rather than silently steering behavior.

mcp.label: MCP
mcp.laymanDefinition: A protocol for exposing tools and context to models and agent clients.
mcp.technicalNote: MCP-style integrations still need capability design, trust boundaries, lifecycle handling, and authorization around each exposed server.

sandbox.label: Sandbox
sandbox.laymanDefinition: An isolated environment that limits what agent actions can reach or change.
sandbox.technicalNote: Sandboxing should constrain files, network, processes, credentials, browser sessions, time, and side effects according to the task risk.

questions.q: What information should persist after this agent run, and who can inspect or correct it?
questions.why: A mistaken memory becomes a durable behavior bug unless it has provenance, scope, and deletion paths.
opts: Dump full transcript into vector search
questions.rot: Store the smallest typed memory that improves future behavior and can be corrected later.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: From memory: which statement best separates agent memory from the context window and RAG?

options.text: Agent memory is durable product state about a user or workflow; the context window is temporary working space; RAG fetches external source content.
Agent memory is anything the model can currently see; the context window is only the system prompt; RAG is another name for memory.
Agent memory is the model’s trained knowledge; the context window is the vector database; RAG stores preferences permanently.
Agent memory, context window, and RAG are interchangeable ways to make the model remember things.

questions.explanation: Memory persists as product state, while context is temporary input and RAG retrieves outside documents or records for the current task.

questions.prompt: A user says, “Please always draft my status updates in bullet points, with risks first.” What type of long-term memory is this best classified as?

options.text: Semantic memory, because it is a factual preference about the user.
Episodic memory, because it records one past conversation.
Procedural memory, because it describes how the agent should perform a recurring task.
Short-term thread state, because it should disappear after the current message.

questions.explanation: A stable instruction about how to do future work is procedural memory because it guides repeated behavior.

questions.prompt: An agent extracts “User has diabetes” from an ambiguous joke in chat and stores it without source details. What is the main failure?

options.text: It used too much namespace isolation.
It turned a low-confidence, sensitive inference into durable state without provenance.
It retrieved too narrowly for the current task.
It should have stored the fact in the context window instead of memory.

questions.explanation: Sensitive or uncertain claims should be filtered or confirmed, and any stored memory needs provenance so it can be audited and corrected.

questions.prompt: During a travel-planning task, the agent has memories about the user’s coding style, coffee preference, passport expiration, and preferred airline seat. Which retrieval behavior is best?

options.text: Retrieve all memories because more personalization is always better.
Retrieve only memories in the travel/user namespace that are relevant to booking, such as passport expiration and seat preference.
Retrieve only the newest memory, regardless of topic.
Do not retrieve any memory; travel planning should only use RAG.

questions.explanation: Good recall uses namespace isolation and task relevance so unrelated memories do not distort the answer.

questions.prompt: Name two user-facing controls or tests that make agent memory safer after it has been written.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Acceptable answers include any two of: a memory viewer/inspection page, correction/edit controls, delete/forget controls, expiration/TTL, user confirmation before storing sensitive memories, tests for failed writes, tests for stale or wrong recall, tests that deleted memories are not retrieved, or tests that irrelevant memories are filtered out.
questions.explanation: Safe memory systems let users see and change stored state, and they test both write failures and recall failures.
